  • 10 Explain the important theories used in pro-social behaviour.
  • Evolutional Psychology Theory - Kin Selection-Rooted in evolutionary biology, Kin Selection
  • Theory posits that pro-social behavior is more likely to occur toward close relatives, as helping
  • them increases the chances of passing on shared genes. The theory is based on the idea of
  • inclusive fitness, meaning individuals help those who share their genetic makeup.
  • Equity-Example: In a romantic relationship, if one partner feels they are contributing more
  • emotionally, financially, or physically than the other without equal returns, they might feel
  • resentment or frustration.
questions.final_answer: resentment or frustration.

questions.question: Explain Social Marketing as a strategy. How does Public Interest Litigation (PIL) function?
questions.solution_html:
• 9 Analyze the causes and consequences of the culture of silence and evaluate its impact as
  • the most pervasive societal barrier
  • a. Fear of authority and repression – People remain silent due to fear of punishment
  • stigma, or social backlash.
  • b. Lack of political empowerment – Limited civic education and participation create
  • passive citizenship.
  • c. Internalized oppression – Marginalized groups begin to believe they have no right or
  • ability to speak.
  • d. Social norms discouraging dissent – Cultural expectations of obedience, hierarchy
  • and respect for elders/authority suppress voice.
  • e. Consequences: perpetuation of inequality – Silence allows exploitation, corruption
  • and injustice to continue unchallenged.
  • f. Weak democratic participation – Low levels of public discussion weaken policy
  • accountability and governance.
  • g. Stagnation of social change – Innovation and reform slow down when people do not
  • question harmful traditions or systems.
  • h. Psychological impacts – Learned helplessness, low self-confidence, and reduced
  • agency become widespread.
  • i. Impact as a societal barrier – Culture of silence becomes embedded across
  • institutions, making collective problem-solving difficult.
  • j. Breaking silence is transformational – Empowerment education, community
  • mobilization, and participatory platforms can shift societies toward justice and
  • awareness.
  • 10 Analyze the interplay between the values and the skills necessary for effective Active
  • Citizenship.
  • a. Values provide motivation – ( justice, empathy, equality, responsibility) create the
  • moral foundation for civic action.
  • b. Skills provide capacity – Communication, negotiation, leadership, and problem
  • solving make civic participation effective.
  • c. Values shape ethical decision-making – Without strong values, civic skills can be
  • misused for personal or political gain.
  • d. Skills operationalize values – Good intentions become meaningful action only when
  • supported by practical abilities.
  • e. Mutual reinforcement – Skills strengthen values by giving individuals confidence to
  • act in alignment with their beliefs.
  • f. Democratic participation requires both – Understanding rights (value) and knowing
  • how to engage (skill) are equally essential.
  • g. Conflict resolution depends on both – Respect (value) must pair with mediation or
  • dialogue skills.
  • h. Community engagement thrives on synergy – Collaborative values (trust
  • cooperation) combine with organizational skills to create impact.
  • i. Citizenship education must integrate both dimensions – Training programs
  • should build civic virtues along with competencies.
  • j. Effective Active Citizenship emerges when values and skills align – Creating
  • informed, empowered, and responsible citizens.
  • 11 Analyze the Youth involvement during Kerala flood, 2018 through the lens of Social
  • Learning Theory and Social Exchange Theory.
  • Social Learning Theory (SLT) perspective

questions.question: Analyze the causes and consequences of the culture of silence and evaluate its impact as the most pervasive societal barrier.
questions.solution_html:
• a. Fear of authority and repression – People remain silent due to fear of punishment
  • stigma, or social backlash.

  • passive citizenship.

  • ability to speak.
  • d. Social norms discouraging dissent – Cultural expectations of obedience, hierarchy
  • and respect for elders/authority suppress voice.
  • e. Consequences: perpetuation of inequality – Silence allows exploitation, corruption
  • and injustice to continue unchallenged.

  • accountability and governance.

  • question harmful traditions or systems.

  • mobilization, and participatory platforms can shift societies toward justice and
  • awareness.

questions.question: Explain the various aspects social exchange with examples. (2 × 10 = 20) END OF THE QUESTION PAPER ***
questions.solution_html:
• Moral Reasoning and Kohlberg's Stages of Moral Development
  • According to Lawrence Kohlberg, moral reasoning develops in stages, and individuals at higher
  • stages are more likely to engage in pro-social behavior because they adhere to ethical principles and
  • values. Pro-social behavior can be seen as an expression of moral values, such as justice, fairness
  • and compassion.
  • Social Exchange Theory suggests that human relationships are formed and maintained based on a
  • cost-benefit analysis, where individuals weigh the potential rewards against the costs of their
  • actions. The theory assumes that people seek to maximize their benefits while minimizing their
  • costs, and that these exchanges are influenced by social norms and expectations.
  • Social Norms and Expectations- Example: In many cultures, there is an unspoken expectation
  • that family members support each other during difficult times (e.g., caring for aging parents), which
  • influences behavior even if the individual’s personal cost is high.
questions.final_answer: influences behavior even if the individual’s personal cost is high.
